title: What Does Balanced Technology Look Like
author: Brett Vogelsinger
summary: Brett Vogelsinger, a high school English teacher in a 1:1 laptop district, audits one real week of his AP Literature and Composition classes to see how much work happens on screens versus paper and people, and why. Responding to the national debate about screen time in schools and his district's new Digital Wellness framework (purposeful, balanced, monitored), he colour-codes his lesson plans and shares analog student work such as sketch-noting a Rumi poem and Writer's Notebook entries. His stated aim is to interrogate the reasons behind each choice rather than fall back on habit. His reflection justifies specific uses: the interactive whiteboard for sharing texts, OneNote for annotation, and laptops for essay revision because of efficiency, version history and the digital form of AP and professional writing, while final copies are printed for analog feedback and major LLMs are blocked. He concludes the week was reasonably balanced, values monitored in-class revision on screens, and identifies a new target: embedding more movement, since screen time impedes it. The piece models teacher-level self-auditing as an alternative to abstract screen-time discourse.
points: Vogelsinger proposes auditing actual lesson plans by marking which activities require screens, turning an abstract debate into a concrete weekly inventory.
He keeps a paper Writer's Notebook central, using analog sketching and poetry routines alongside digital tools.
Essay revision on laptops is defended for efficiency, version history and language tools, and because students' high-stakes and professional writing will be digital.
Revision on screens is better done in class, where students can be monitored, ask questions and use peers as beta readers, which reduces rushed revision at home.
His main takeaway is that a largely sedentary, screen-inclusive week needs deliberate movement built into long block periods.
quotes: I am a high school English teacher working in a 1:1 district, and laptops have become what binders were for me and my classmates of yesteryear: an active space to organize and accomplish and create things for school.

The start of this year seemed like a good time to take an honest inventory of the classwork and homework I ask students to do and interrogate how much of it is on paper and how much of it is on a screen. More importantly, I want to make sure I am thinking through the reason for those choices to avoid simply falling back on habits.
On average, teens spend 8+ hours a day on screens. In any conversation about technology at school for learning purposes, let’s first acknowledge that students spend a lot their free time on screens.

Revising essays on laptops also makes sense. It provides efficiency, a version history that records the writing process, and language tools like voice-to-text, Editor, and spell check. Some on-demand writing on paper will happen this year, but that is a different skill set.

I like that some of their revision process happens on a screen but in a classroom where students can be monitored, ask questions, and have access to each other as beta readers. This helps keep us honest, engaged, and relieves some of the pressure that can rush a revision process at home.
But this was a mostly sedentary week, and I want to keep ideas for embedding movement, especially in lengthy learning blocks, at the front of my weekly planning.

But I’m also sure that tuning into what this balance looks like for one short week will be instructive to me in my future planning. Cogs will turn in the background of my brain as I plan with this interrogative post in mind.
